cards.text: Job, a man the LORD called blameless and upright (Job 2:3), is covered in boils, and his own wife has told him, “Curse God and die!” (Job 2:7, 9). His three friends have sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, and nobody has said a word (Job 2:13). After this, Job finally opens his mouth.

cards.question: Job's wife told him to curse God. When Job finally opens his mouth, what does he curse?

cards.text: Job says, “May the day of my birth perish, and the night it was said, ‘A boy is conceived.’” Friend, most people want a party on their birthday, and Job wants his to PERISH.

cards.question: Job wants the day he was born to perish. What does he ask God above to do with that day?
Job wishes the day he was born had turned to darkness.

cards.text: Job keeps piling it on: darkness and gloom, a cloud settling over that day, blackness to overwhelm it. That's not asking for a little shade, friend, that's ordering the FULL blackout package.
Then he goes after the night too: if only darkness had taken that night away! And may it never show up among the days of the year or in any of the months.

cards.question: Job wants the night he was conceived wiped off the calendar for good. What is he really wishing for?

answers.text: That he had never been born
That he could start the year over
That his friends would leave him alone

cards.question: Job wants the night he was conceived to be full of joyful voices.

cards.text: He even wants that night cursed by those who curse the day, the ones prepared to rouse Leviathan. Job is holding NOTHING back.

cards.question: Job wants that night's morning stars to go dark, and he wants the night to wait in vain for ___.
Job finally says why he's cursing the night he was conceived. What's his reason?

answers.text: It let him be born to see sorrow
It brought bad luck on his family
It came during a time of famine

cards.text: Job's cursed the day and he's cursed the night. Now the why questions start, and the first one is a heavy one: why didn't he die the moment he was born?
Why were there knees to receive him, and someone there to nurse him? I think every bit of care he got as a baby feels like a question mark to him now.

cards.question: Job says that if he had died at birth, he'd be lying down right now. What would he have?
Job pictures himself at rest among those who have already died. Who does he say he'd be lying there with?
Job says the kings and counselors lying at rest built cities that are still standing strong.

cards.text: Or, Job says, he'd be with princes who had gold and filled their houses with silver.
Then Job asks why he wasn't hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees the light. I think this one hurts, friend.

cards.question: Job says that where the dead lie, even the wicked stop their raging.
In that place where the dead lie, Job says captives still hear the voice of the oppressor.
Job says small and great are both in that place where the dead lie, and there the slave is ___ from his master.

cards.text: Then Job asks a bigger why, about more than just himself. Why is light given to the miserable, people who long for death that doesn't come and search for it like hidden treasure?

cards.question: Job describes miserable people who long for death that does not come. When they finally reach the grave, how does he say they feel?

cards.text: Then Job turns it back on himself: why is life given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?

cards.question: Job describes his days now. He says that when food is put before him, he ___.

cards.text: And Job's groans pour out like water. I think that's a man whose sorrow just won't shut off, like a faucet stuck wide open.

cards.question: Job says the trouble he dreaded has stayed far away from him.

cards.text: Job ends with this: “I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest, for trouble has come.” Job's said his piece, friend, but this story is a LONG way from over.
